catalog_quote: 0.3.2. El acento prosódico Cada palabra tiene una sílaba que está acentuada, o sea, se pronuncia con una intensidad mayor que las otras sílabas de la palabra. Esta sílaba es generalmente la última de la raíz de la palabra y no se indica con un acento escrito. qui-tscu marrano to-tsi-nein estaba hablando qui-so-jndëë venado La última sílaba de la raíz de una palabra se acentúa tanto si va al final de la palabra como si va seguida por un sufijo. En los siguientes ejemplos la sílaba acentuada va seguida por un sufijo: tachi-hö' mi abuelito toju'-hin él estaba brincando En algunos nombres del español y otros préstamos que tienen acento ortográfico, se retiene éste al usarlos en amuzgo. Maríaha' María tëcafé tseon semilla del quimbombó cominsiónhin' los policías

new_statements.quote: 0.3.2. El acento prosódico. Cada palabra tiene una sílaba que está acentuada, o sea, se pronuncia con una intensidad mayor que las otras sílabas de la palabra. Esta sílaba es generalmente la última de la raíz de la palabra y no se indica con un acento escrito. [...] La última sílaba de la raíz de una palabra se acentúa tanto si va al final de la palabra como si va seguida por un sufijo. [...] En algunos nombres del español y otros préstamos que tienen acento ortográfico, se retiene éste al usarlos en amuzgo.
new_statements.translation: 0.3.2. Prosodic stress. Every word has one syllable that is stressed, i.e. pronounced with greater intensity than the other syllables of the word. This syllable is generally the last syllable of the root of the word and is not marked with a written accent. [...] The last syllable of the root of a word is stressed whether it is word-final or is followed by a suffix. [...] In some Spanish names and other loanwords that carry an orthographic accent, that accent is retained when they are used in Amuzgo.

Stewart (recopiladores), Diccionario amuzgo de San Pedro Amuzgos, Oaxaca (Serie de vocabularios y diccionarios indígenas "Mariano Silva y Aceves" 44), pp. 361-480. new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Rendered PDF page 390 of (page render, 150 dpi) and read the image: printed page number 371, running head "0. La fonología", section "0.3.2. El acento prosódico". The three quoted prose passages are on that page word for word: "Cada palabra tiene una sílaba que está acentuada, o sea, se pronuncia con una intensidad mayor que las otras sílabas de la palabra. Esta sílaba es generalmente la última de la raíz de la palabra y no se indica con un acento escrito." / "La última sílaba de la raíz de una palabra se acentúa tanto si va al final de la palabra como si va seguida por un sufijo." / "En algunos nombres del español y otros préstamos que tienen acento ortográfico, se retiene éste al usarlos…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stressed syllable per word; it is the last syllable of the root (roots are mostly monosyllabic, prefixes precede it), regardless of whether suffixes/enclitics follow. Examples given: qui-tscu 'pig', to-tsi-nein 'was speaking', qui-so-jndéé 'deer' (stress on the final root syllable); tachi-hó 'my grandfather', toju'-hin 'he was jumping' (stressed root syllable followed by a suffix). Hernández Hernández (2019: 80-81) independently finds, by vowel duration, that in compounds stress falls on the second (final) root syllable ('sistema yámbico', weak-strong), with pretonic syllables about half the duration of tonic ones (p. 144).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Spanish loans and names keep their Spanish stress (e.g. María, café, comisión) (Buck 2000: 371). Kim (2022: 536) adds that Spanish loans receive an H-L tone melody anchored to the Spanish-stressed syllable. Buck 2000 says 'generalmente' (generally) the last root syllable, without listing native exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (the stressed syllable is defined per word, including prefix+root+suffix strings); tone (8 tones per Kim 2022, 7 per Hernández Hernández 2019) is independent and contrastive; Buck notes the tilde in the orthography marks the 1PL exclusive tone (high-low glide), not stress. The source predates instrumental work; Hernández Hernández 2019 is duration-based on compounds and clitic groups.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement is from the grammar sketch "Gramática amuzga de San Pedro Amuzgos, Oax." by Marjorie J. Buck, printed inside Stewart & Stewart (2000), the SIL dictionary of the San Pedro Amuzgos variety (= sanp1260; Glottolog lists this book under Stewart & Stewart 2000 as a grammar sketch). The dictionary's introduction notes Buck's earlier work was on Xochistlahuaca (Guerrero) Amuzgo (guer1243), but the sketch is explicitly of San Pedro Amuzgos. Kim (2022) cites the same sketch as "Buck 2000". The supporting thesis (Hernández Hernández 2019) is by a native speaker of San Pedro Amuzgos.

tone_statements.citation: Kim, Yuni. 2026. Fonología amuzga: Experiencia personal de una exploración del habla de San Pedro Amuzgos. Lingüística Mexicana. Nueva Época 8(2) [número temático 'La investigación del amuzgo. Entre la academia y las comunidades']: 1-15. doi:10.62190/amla.lmne.2026.8.2.621
tone_statements.quote: En este análisis registro tres tonos de nivel: alto (5), medio (3) y bajo (1), y dos tonos de contorno: ascendente (35) y descendente (31). De acuerdo con Trubetzkoy (2019 [1939], pág. 280) una lengua que cuenta moras es aquella en la que la unidad prosódica no coincide necesariamente con la sílaba sino con la mora, en el amuzgo de AZG la Unidad Portadora de Tono (UPT) es la mora µ. Cada mora se puede asociar a uno de los cinco tonos fonológicos de esta variante de a cuerdo con la Well-formedness Condition (WFC)(Goldsmith, 1976).
tone_statements.translation: In this analysis I record three level tones: high (5), mid (3) and low (1), and two contour tones: rising (35) and falling (31). Following Trubetzkoy ... a mora-counting language is one in which the prosodic unit does not necessarily coincide with the syllable but with the mora; in AZG Amuzgo the Tone-Bearing Unit (TBU) is the mora. Each mora can be associated with one of the five phonological tones of this variety in accordance with the Well-formedness Condition (Goldsmith 1976).
tone_statements.summary: Five tones (H, M, L, rising 35, falling 31) in Chao numerals, mora as TBU; bimoraic nuclei may carry tone sequences. Author rejects the ballistic/controlled syllable distinction; corpus recorded and transcribed in Praat.

tone_statements.citation: Cortés Vázquez, Mariela. 2023. Fonología y procesos fonológicos en la formación de sustantivos en el amuzgo de San Pedro Amuzgos, Oaxaca. In Marcela San Giacomo, Fidel Hernández & Michael Swanton (eds.), Estudios sobre lenguas mixtecanas, pp. 293-319. México: Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Antropológicas.
tone_statements.quote: A diferencia del español, en amuzgo (y muchas otras lenguas de la región), el tono de cada sílaba es contrastivo -se puede decir hasta “fonémico”- porque el significado de la palabra depende no solo del conjunto de consonantes y vocales, sino también del tono. En el diccionario de Tapia García (1999), y también en los materiales del Instituto Lingüístico de Verano (Buck 2000, Stewart y Stewart 2000), se reconocían ocho tonos distintos que una sílaba podía llevar. [...] Smith-Stark y Tapia García (1984) reconocieron las mismas categorías, y las anotaban con números de 1 (nivel bajo) a 5 (nivel alto), que se siguieron usando en el diccionario de Tapia García (1999).
tone_statements.translation: Unlike Spanish, in Amuzgo (and many other languages of the region) the tone of each syllable is contrastive - one could even say 'phonemic' - because the meaning of the word depends not only on the set of consonants and vowels but also on the tone. In Tapia García's dictionary (1999), and also in the SIL materials (Buck 2000, Stewart & Stewart 2000), eight distinct tones that a syllable could bear were recognised. [...] Smith-Stark & Tapia García (1984) recognised the same categories and wrote them with numbers from 1 (low level) to 5 (high level), which continued to be used in Tapia García's dictionary (1999).
tone_statements.locator: section on tones, immediately before and around examples (11)-(18) (XML galley, unpaginated; article pp. 1-15)
tone_statements.summary: Syllable-based lexical tone with eight contrastive categories (Tapia/Smith-Stark 5, 53, 35, 34, 3, 31, 12, 1 = SIL alto, alto-medio, medio-alto, medio-medio, medio, alto-bajo, bajo-bajo, bajo), the 34/12 categories longer and slightly rising; ongoing change in younger speakers (53 > extra-high level, 31 > very high slightly falling) and incipient contextual raising of low after high.

tone_statements.citation: Cortés Vázquez, Mariela. 2021. Procesos morfofonológicos en la flexión de número nominal en el amuzgo de San Pedro Amuzgos, Oaxaca. Tesis de maestría (Maestría en Antropología, Programa de Posgrado en Antropología, FFyL/IIA), Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México. 143 pp. Asesor: Samuel Herrera Castro. hdl:20.500.14330/TES01000806731
tone_statements.quote: Como es típico en la familia otomangue el amuzgo es una lengua tonal, con 11 tonos distintos en Xochistlahuaca (Bauernschmidt, 1965) y 8 tonos en San Pedro Amuzgos (Smith-Stark y Tapia García, 1984). ... Según Buck (2000), los 8 patrones prosódicos en sílabas de esta variante se reducen a 5 tonos, con contraste controlado-balístico en tres de ellos ... Smith-Stark y Tapia García (1984) identifican ocho tonos: tres nivelados (alto, medio, bajo), tres ascendentes (medio-alto, medio, bajo), y dos descendentes (alto, medio).
tone_statements.translation: As is typical in the Otomanguean family, Amuzgo is a tonal language, with 11 distinct tones in Xochistlahuaca (Bauernschmidt 1965) and 8 tones in San Pedro Amuzgos (Smith-Stark & Tapia Garcia 1984). ... According to Buck (2000), the 8 prosodic patterns on syllables of this variety reduce to 5 tones, with a controlled-ballistic contrast in three of them ... Smith-Stark & Tapia Garcia (1984) identify eight tones: three level (high, mid, low), three rising (mid-high, mid, low), and two falling (high, mid).
tone_statements.locator: p. 1 sec. 1 Introduccion and p. 2 sec. 1 / sec. 2.1 Previos trabajos
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: 8 tones, Praat f0 description from one speaker; low-tone sandhi after high/mid-high; 8 tones vs 5 tones+ballisticity vs register analysis left open. Stress remark (root-final) reported from Buck.

tone_statements.quote: Tabla 1. Inventario tonal del amuzgo de San Pedro Amuzgos ... bajo 1 cha ‘tortilla’ (forma reducida) / medio 2 ta ‘grueso’ / alto 3 ta ‘lleno de maleza’ / extra-alto 4 ta ‘Don, señor’ / medio-alto 23 tan ‘chueco’ / medio-bajo 21 ta ‘bordo, mecapal’ / alto-medio 32 ta ‘cantamos (incl.)’ / Fuente: Elaboración propia con datos tomados de Hernández (2019, p. 171) ... Por último, se trata de una lengua que cuenta con una alta complejidad tonal y grados de laringización. Esta variante de amuzgo presenta un inventario de cuatro tonos de nivel y tres tonos de contorno; véase la tabla 1.
tone_statements.translation: Table 1. Tone inventory of San Pedro Amuzgos Amuzgo ... low 1 cha 'tortilla' (reduced form) / mid 2 ta 'thick' / high 3 ta 'full of weeds' / extra-high 4 ta 'Don, sir' / mid-high 23 tan 'crooked' / mid-low 21 ta 'ridge, tumpline' / high-mid 32 ta 'we sing (incl.)' / Source: authors' elaboration with data from Hernández (2019, p. 171) ... Finally, it is a language with high tonal complexity and degrees of laryngealization. This variety of Amuzgo has an inventory of four level tones and three contour tones; see Table 1.
tone_statements.locator: p. 36 Tabla 1 and p. 37 'Aspectos generales de la lengua'
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: 4 level + 3 contour tones written as digits, inventory after Hernández 2019; own data: tone on the noun root alone marks 1st/2nd-person possession, docking on the last syllable of the melodic group.

tone_statements.citation: Smith-Stark, Thomas C. & Fermín Tapia García. 2017. Amuzgo de San Pedro Amuzgos, Oaxaca. Archivo de Lenguas Indígenas de México. México: El Colegio de México. 241 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Tonos /5/ tono alto de nivel ... /53/ tono que desciende levemente del nivel alto hacia el nivel medio ... /35/ tono que sube lentamente del nivel medio hacia el nivel alto ... /34/ tono de nivel medio que sube ligeramente ... /3/ tono de nivel medio que baja levemente hacia su terminación ... /31/ tono descendente que se inicia en un nivel medio alto y cae violentamente hacia el nivel bajo ... /12/ tono de nivel bajo que sube levemente ... /1/ tono de nivel bajo que baja levemente hacia su terminación
tone_statements.translation: Tones /5/ high level tone ... /53/ tone that falls slightly from the high level toward the mid level ... /35/ tone that rises slowly from the mid level toward the high level ... /34/ mid level tone that rises slightly ... /3/ mid level tone that falls slightly toward its end ... /31/ falling tone that starts at a mid-high level and drops sharply to the low level ... /12/ low level tone that rises slightly ... /1/ low level tone that falls slightly toward its end
tone_statements.locator: Fonología: Fonemas: Tonos, pp. 33-34; prologue '8 tonos distintivos' p. 9; syllable/tone statement Fonotáctica p. 43
tone_statements.summary: Eight tonemes written as pitch numbers (5 high-1 low), each illustrated; minimal sets tan/ta/jna etc. pp. 40-42; at least 100 tone-marked forms. Stress final, phonetic, non-contrastive; enclitics atonic. No sandhi/downstep discussed.

tone_statements.citation: Buck, Marjorie J. 2014. San Pedro Amuzgos Paradigms [paradigm files for all parts of speech, with 'Amz-SPA Paradigms Explanations 2014']. Manuscript, draft (posted as is), 559 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 58138 (SIL Mexico). File,https://www.sil.org/resources/archives/58138
tone_statements.quote: a letter, or letters, is given in parentheses to indicate the tone of each syllable of the word. The syllables are ballistic or controlled [...] Tones are symbolized as follows: (a-m) alto-medio high tone, ballistic syllable (a) alto high tone, controlled syllable (m) medio mid tone, ballistic syllable (m-m) medio-medio mid tone, controlled syllable (b) bajo low tone, ballistic syllable (b-b) bajo-bajo low tone, controlled syllable (a-b) alto-bajo high-low glide, ballistic syllable (m-a) medio-alto mid-high glide, controlled syllable [...] Nouns, verbs and other words which indicate grammatical person, may undergo changes for tone.
tone_statements.locator: Explanations, 'Tone and syllable type', pp. 2-3 and 'Tone patterns', p. 8
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones plus high-low and mid-high glides, cross-classified by ballistic vs controlled syllable into eight marked categories per syllable; lexical and grammatical (person/number inflection replaces the tone of nouns and verbs; 1pl.excl always high-low).

tone_statements.citation: Bartholomew, Doris A. 2000. Lexicography of two Amuzgo dictionaries [comparison of Tapia García 1999 and Stewart & Stewart 2000, Amuzgo of San Pedro Amuzgos]. Language and Culture Archives, Bartholomew Collection of Unpublished Materials, SIL International - Mexico Branch, entry 77271. 22 pp. (draft).
tone_statements.quote: The two analyses recognize the same number of tone contrasts. The Stewart analysis (following that of Bauernschmidt for Xochistlahuaca) distinguishes ballistic and controlled syllables (written with a double vowel in most cases; length is less noticeable in pre-stress syllables). Each syllable type has high, mid and low tones and one contour tone. The Tapia (with Smith-Stark) analysis writes several contour tones in addition to the high, mid and low level tones [Low tone is 1; hight tone is 5].
tone_statements.locator: section 'Tones', p. 5, with the Stewart/Tapia correspondence table
tone_statements.summary: Eight tone contrasts per syllable in both SPA analyses: {high, mid, low, one contour} x {ballistic, controlled} (Stewart) = 5, 53, 35, 34, 3, 31, 12, 1 (Tapia/Smith-Stark).

tone.translation: Unlike Spanish, in Amuzgo (and many other languages of the region) the tone of each syllable is contrastive - one could even say 'phonemic' - because the meaning of the word depends not only on the set of consonants and vowels but also on the tone. In Tapia García's dictionary (1999), and also in the SIL materials (Buck 2000, Stewart & Stewart 2000), eight distinct tones that a syllable could bear were recognised. [...] Smith-Stark & Tapia García (1984) recognised the same categories and wrote them with numbers from 1 (low level) to 5 (high level), which continued to be used in Tapia García's dictionary (1999).
tone.summary: Syllable-based lexical tone with eight contrastive categories (Tapia/Smith-Stark 5, 53, 35, 34, 3, 31, 12, 1 = SIL alto, alto-medio, medio-alto, medio-medio, medio, alto-bajo, bajo-bajo, bajo), the 34/12 categories longer and slightly rising; ongoing change in younger speakers (53 > extra-high level, 31 > very high slightly falling) and incipient contextual raising of low after high.
tone.says: Read in full from the journal's XML galley (download/621/773; text kept at work_2026-09-20/tb4/sanp1260/, not mirrored because a tone statement is already listed here). States that every syllable carries a contrastive ('phonemic') tone; that Tapia García 1999, Buck 2000 and Stewart & Stewart 2000 recognise eight tones per syllable, the same categories as Smith-Stark & Tapia 1984 (numbered 1 low to 5 high); walks through the categories with word lists: 'alto' = 5, 'medio-alto'/ascendente = 35, '…

sources.quote: Como es típico en la familia otomangue el amuzgo es una lengua tonal, con 11 tonos distintos en Xochistlahuaca (Bauernschmidt, 1965) y 8 tonos en San Pedro Amuzgos (Smith-Stark y Tapia García, 1984). ... tone.translation: As is typical in the Otomanguean family, Amuzgo is a tonal language, with 11 distinct tones in Xochistlahuaca (Bauernschmidt 1965) and 8 tones in San Pedro Amuzgos (Smith-Stark & Tapia Garcia 1984). ... According to Buck (2000), the 8 prosodic patterns on syllables of this variety reduce to 5 tones, with a controlled-ballistic contrast in three of them ... Smith-Stark & Tapia Garcia (1984) identify eight tones: three level (high, mid, low), three rising (mid-high, mid, low), and two falling (high, mid).

sources.quote: The two analyses recognize the same number of tone contrasts. The Stewart analysis (following that of Bauernschmidt for Xochistlahuaca) distinguishes ballistic and controlled syllables (written with a double vowel in most cases; length is less noticeable in pre-stress syllables). Each syllable type has high, mid and low tones and one contour tone. The Tapia (with Smith-Stark) analysis writes several contour tones in addition to the high, mid and low level tones [Low tone is 1; hight tone is 5].
sources.locator: section 'Tones', p. 5, with the Stewart/Tapia correspondence table
sources.note: Read from the copy. The 'Tones' section (p. 5) states that the two analyses recognise the same number of tone contrasts: Stewart (following Bauernschmidt) distinguishes ballistic and controlled syllables, each with high, mid, low and one contour tone; Tapia/Smith-Stark write level tones plus several contours on a 1 (low) to 5 (high) scale; a correspondence table equates controlled (a)=5, (m-m)=34, (b-b)=12, (m-a)=35 and ballistic (a-m)=53, (m)=3, (b)=1, (a-b)=31; notes that Tapia's practical diacritics (acute = 5, circumflex = 31, grave = 1, rest unmarked) under-distinguish tone sets.

tone.translation: Tones /5/ high level tone ... /53/ tone that falls slightly from the high level toward the mid level ... /35/ tone that rises slowly from the mid level toward the high level ... /34/ mid level tone that rises slightly ... /3/ mid level tone that falls slightly toward its end ... /31/ falling tone that starts at a mid-high level and drops sharply to the low level ... /12/ low level tone that rises slightly ... /1/ low level tone that falls slightly toward its end
